what a request actually costs

A server request has four phases; this report times the first two. search finds the matching suffixes, retrieval turns them into protein references — and then decode unpacks each hit's annotations and serialise writes the JSON that goes back to the caller. Every throughput number in this report, in every suite, is phases 1-2 only. Only defaults pays to measure phases 3-4 at all, and this is where they are reported.

The grid below is one number per cell: what percentage of a request the timed phases were. 90% means search and retrieval dominate and a knob that speeds them up reaches the caller almost undiluted. 10% means the request is nearly all decode and JSON, and the same knob buys a tenth of what it appears to. The share collapses as the answer grows — a short non-tryptic peptide matches half the database and spends its time serialising the result, while a long tryptic one matches almost nothing and spends it all in search.

bounds and iter are shares of search THREAD-time, which is summed across every rayon thread and so exceeds wall time by the parallelism factor in the last column — they are meaningful against each other, not against the clock. Which of the two dominates is what decides whether a prefetch distance ever had a phase to work on; see prefetch.

Suite notes

This is the sweep to run after any change to the search path, and the only one to run on every commit. It answers ONE question — what does this version do at the settings that ship — and it answers it at high precision, which is what makes a delta against a baseline mean something.

Everything is held at the production configuration except the two SEARCH OPTIONS, equate_il and tryptic, which are not tuning at all: they are what the caller asked for. Both are in production use, they change the shape of the search rather than its parameters, and a regression that only shows up under one of them is a regression this suite has to catch. Four rows per length regime.

What is deliberately NOT here, and where it went:

  • the k-mer tables -> run.sh kmer
  • the MLP batch curve -> run.sh mlp
  • validate_batch -> run.sh validate
  • the prefetch distances -> run.sh prefetch

Those used to be folded in, which made this suite a 34-row grid that took six times as long and re-measured settled questions on every commit. The split is not just cheaper: a regression gate and a parameter sweep want opposite things from a run. The gate wants few cells at high precision so a 3% move is visible; the sweep wants many cells at whatever precision fits the budget. One grid cannot be both, and when it tried, it was the gate that lost.

Read the noise column before the mmap/pre column. The measured run-to-run noise floor on the full database is 3.9%, and any delta below that — or below a cell's own measured band — is noise, not signal.

Held values are not assumed: the run records every SearchTuning field and the summary prints back what these cells actually ran at. If that line does not read the shipped values, this run was not measuring the defaults.

Suite notes

One question: is the k-mer table worth attaching, and if so, which one. Everything else is held at the production configuration, so a difference in a row is the table and nothing else.

The mechanism is why this is a suite of its own rather than a column in defaults. A search without a table binary-searches the suffix array from scratch: a dependent chain of pointer-chasing probes, each one a cache miss that cannot be prefetched because its address depends on the previous probe's result. A k-mer table skips the first k levels of that chain by looking the prefix up directly. So the table's value is a FUNCTION OF PEPTIDE LENGTH — it removes a fixed number of probes, which is a large share of a short peptide's work and a small share of a long one's. Reading one number for "the k-mer table" averages that away, which is why every row here is per length regime.

equate_il is HELD at the shipped value here; only tryptic is swept. The two are not equivalent contexts, and the instrumented arm in defaults is what settles it — with I/L equated or not, the search examines about the same candidates (1.26M against 1.15M) and accepts about the same share of them (10.7% against 11.0%), and the binary-search/range-scan split barely moves (46/54 against 42/58). Under tryptic all three change at once: 9x fewer candidates, acceptance down to ~2%, and the split inverts to 86/14. So tryptic is a different workload and earns its multiplication; equate_il is the same workload with a different answer, which is a question for defaults and nowhere else. Crossing it here cost 45% of the whole sweep and moved a resolved k-mer winner in 2 of 23 contexts.

Read the table this way:

  • vs none is the column that decides. A table that does not clear its row's floor is not a small win, it is no answer — and it still costs its resident bytes.
  • table GB beside it, always. The 6-mer is 2.85 GB resident against the 5-mer's 0.12 GB, a 24x cost, and this suite runs UNCONSTRAINED, which is the one regime where that cost is invisible. A 6-mer that wins by less than the floor is a loss. The table GB column is computed from k, not measured — the table is dense at 24^k entries of 16 bytes — and it has to be, because one matrix process loads every k the grid names before it sweeps, so process RSS is identical in every row and can attribute nothing.
  • the two backends should agree on the SIGN. The table shortens the probe chain, which is a property of the search rather than of the storage; if mmap and preloaded disagree about whether a table helps, something else moved.

The verdict this suite is currently expected to reproduce, from the last full-database run: with the index resident, the 6-mer is inside the noise floor on medium/small and only +4.1% on large, for 2.85 GB against 0.12 GB — so the 5-mer ships and the 6-mer does not. That verdict does NOT hold under a memory ceiling, where the table's value is working-set size rather than probe count and the 6-mer reaches +18.4% against no table. See ram for the capped answer; this suite deliberately does not sweep ceilings, because a table comparison under a cap is a different experiment with a root requirement attached.

Suite notes

One question: how many independent peptide searches should be interleaved per rayon task. That is mlp_batch, the CROSS-QUERY batch — B=1 is the scalar path, and DEFAULT_MLP_BATCH is what search_all_peptides passes on every server request. It is not the same knob as SearchTuning::validate_batch, which batches candidate suffixes WITHIN one range scan; that one belongs to validate; the two crossed are mlp_validate.

The k-mer table is held at the shipped 5-mer. Crossing the batch with the tables is a different question — whether the three accelerators are separable — and combos asks it.

The mechanism: a suffix-array probe is a random read whose address depends on the previous probe's result, so a single search is a dependent chain of cache misses with nothing to overlap. Batching B searches per task gives the memory system B independent chains at once, and the win is however much of that latency the hardware can then hide.

Which means the curve's shape is a property of WHAT IS LIMITING the machine, and that is the thing to read here:

  • a curve that rises and plateaus says memory-level parallelism was the constraint and batching found it.
  • a curve that is flat says something else is the wall. On the full database that has been the measured answer — +4% peaking at B=16 against +57% on swissprot — because a 242 GB working set misses the TLB on every access and there are only ~2-4 hardware page walkers per core, so the per-core parallelism is capped there no matter how many data prefetches are in flight.
  • a curve that rises and then FALLS puts the top of the useful range at the peak; past it the per-step bookkeeping costs more than the overlap saves.

Expect the answer to differ by peptide length and to differ between swissprot and the full database. It is measured per bucket for that reason, and the value that ships has to win the mixed reality, not the friendliest bucket.

This is the only measurement of the curve. A second, instrumented one used to live in a detail suite; its counters perturbed throughput by ~2% and it swept one peptide file, so it was a worse copy of this. What only the counters can produce — the binary-search/range-scan split behind the curve — is now one instrumented arm inside defaults.

equate_il is HELD at the shipped value here; only tryptic is swept. The two are not equivalent contexts, and the instrumented arm in defaults is what settles it — with I/L equated or not, the search examines about the same candidates (1.26M against 1.15M) and accepts about the same share of them (10.7% against 11.0%), and the binary-search/range-scan split barely moves (46/54 against 42/58). Under tryptic all three change at once: 9x fewer candidates, acceptance down to ~2%, and the split inverts to 86/14. So tryptic is a different workload and earns its multiplication; equate_il is the same workload with a different answer, which is a question for defaults and nowhere else. Crossing it here cost 45% of the whole sweep and moved a resolved k-mer winner in 2 of 23 contexts.

validate_batch holds candidate suffixes in flight while their text is compared, so it exists to cover one memory latency and stops paying once it does — a cliff, not a peak. It is the second of two batches: mlp_batch interleaves whole peptide searches, this one interleaves candidates within a single range scan. Both consume the same line-fill buffers, which is why mlp_validate crosses them.

Suite notes

One knob: SearchTuning::validate_batch, the number of candidate suffixes processed per two-pass batch inside iterate_sa_range. It is NOT the cross-query batch — that is mlp_batch, and mlp owns it. This one batches within a single peptide's range scan; that one batches across peptides. The two crossed are mlp_validate.

Expect a CLIFF, not a peak. The established result is that 16 -> 32 buys about 10% and the curve plateaus above it: the batch exists to hold enough candidate reads in flight to cover one memory latency, and once it does, more does nothing. A peak in the middle of the range is therefore suspicious and usually means the process drifted — read the resolution table first.

equate_il is HELD at the shipped value here; only tryptic is swept. The two are not equivalent contexts, and the instrumented arm in defaults is what settles it — with I/L equated or not, the search examines about the same candidates (1.26M against 1.15M) and accepts about the same share of them (10.7% against 11.0%), and the binary-search/range-scan split barely moves (46/54 against 42/58). Under tryptic all three change at once: 9x fewer candidates, acceptance down to ~2%, and the split inverts to 86/14. So tryptic is a different workload and earns its multiplication; equate_il is the same workload with a different answer, which is a question for defaults and nowhere else. Crossing it here cost 45% of the whole sweep and moved a resolved k-mer winner in 2 of 23 contexts.

Suite notes

Two knobs, one mechanism at two points in the search:

  • prefetch_threshold — how large a candidate range has to be before the two-pass validation path is used at all, rather than a straight scan.
  • retrieval_prefetch_distance — how far ahead the retrieval loop issues its hints while walking the matched suffixes.

Both are software prefetch distances, so both are bets on how far ahead the hardware needs to be told about a load. A distance too short does not cover the latency; too long and the line is evicted before it is used, or the extra hints displace something useful. The interesting shape is therefore a plateau with soft edges, and the useful answer is usually "anywhere in the middle".

Swept as a full 4x4 cross rather than two curves, which is honest at sixteen points and lets the report say whether the two distances interact — they are consuming the same hardware, so a plane costs almost nothing extra and is the only way to find out.

  • This suite is expected to conclude that neither knob pays. Both read flat in every context measured so far, and docs/design/README.md records that scalar k-mer prefetch was already killed for the same reason: median +0.3%, inside the noise floor, removed rather than left as a knob. A run that confirms flatness across both length regimes and both backends is grounds for deleting these two fields from SearchTuning — which is the point of running it. Read the resolution table first: a process whose residual is wider than the effects below it has not shown flatness, it has shown nothing.

equate_il is HELD at the shipped value here; only tryptic is swept. The two are not equivalent contexts, and the instrumented arm in defaults is what settles it — with I/L equated or not, the search examines about the same candidates (1.26M against 1.15M) and accepts about the same share of them (10.7% against 11.0%), and the binary-search/range-scan split barely moves (46/54 against 42/58). Under tryptic all three change at once: 9x fewer candidates, acceptance down to ~2%, and the split inverts to 86/14. So tryptic is a different workload and earns its multiplication; equate_il is the same workload with a different answer, which is a question for defaults and nowhere else. Crossing it here cost 45% of the whole sweep and moved a resolved k-mer winner in 2 of 23 contexts.

The ridge drawn on each plane is the result. If the best mlp_batch is not the same at every validate_batch, the two knobs interact and neither mlp nor validate can be read on its own; if it holds, both curves are sufficient and this suite need not be run again until the search path changes.

Suite notes

The two batches crossed. mlp and validate each own one of them as a curve against a fixed background; this suite is the plane those two curves are slices through, and it exists because there is a specific reason to think the slices are not the whole picture.

The mechanism: both knobs hold in-flight misses. mlp_batch interleaves whole peptide searches per rayon task; validate_batch interleaves candidate suffixes inside one range scan. They stack — the misses outstanding at any moment go roughly as their PRODUCT — against a fixed number of line-fill buffers per core. Past that limit the extra requests queue rather than overlap, so the best value of each should depend on the other, and the ridge through the plane should run diagonally.

That is the whole question: is the ridge diagonal? If it is, neither curve can be read on its own and the pair has to be chosen together. If the peak sits at the same mlp_batch for every validate_batch, the two are separable and mlp and validate are sufficient.

equate_il is HELD at the shipped value here; only tryptic is swept. The two are not equivalent contexts, and the instrumented arm in defaults is what settles it — with I/L equated or not, the search examines about the same candidates (1.26M against 1.15M) and accepts about the same share of them (10.7% against 11.0%), and the binary-search/range-scan split barely moves (46/54 against 42/58). Under tryptic all three change at once: 9x fewer candidates, acceptance down to ~2%, and the split inverts to 86/14. So tryptic is a different workload and earns its multiplication; equate_il is the same workload with a different answer, which is a question for defaults and nowhere else. Crossing it here cost 45% of the whole sweep and moved a resolved k-mer winner in 2 of 23 contexts.

Related but not the same: combos adds the k-mer table as a third axis at a coarser resolution, and asks whether all three accelerators are simultaneously reachable. This suite is the fine-grained two-knob picture.

Suite notes

The one deliberately MULTIPLICATIVE suite in the harness, and the only one that needs to be.

kmer, mlp and validate each sweep their own knob against a fixed background, which answers "what is this knob's curve" at a cost that adds rather than multiplies. What they cannot answer is whether the three optima are simultaneously reachable — a set of one-at-a-time winners is only the best configuration if the knobs do not interact, and here there is reason to think they might:

  • the k-mer table removes most of the binary search's probes, which is most of what mlp_batch was overlapping. Batching has less latency to hide once a table is attached.
  • mlp_batch and validate_batch both hold misses in flight, against a fixed number of line-fill buffers per core, so their outstanding misses go roughly as their PRODUCT.
  • the table changes which of the two phases dominates, and the two batches live in different phases.

So the axes are deliberately coarse — three values each, not the full curves — because the question is whether the peak MOVES, not where exactly it sits. kmer, mlp and validate own the resolution; this suite owns the corners.

All four equate_il x tryptic combinations, mixed only. Adding the length regimes on top would be a second multiplication for a suite that is already the expensive one, and defaults reports what each regime costs at the shipped tuple.

Read the winners table first. If every context picks the same tuple, the three knobs are separable and their individual suites can be trusted on their own. If the winner moves, the tuple that ships has to be chosen for the context that matters, and the individual curves are each reporting one slice through a surface.

equate_il is HELD at the shipped value here; only tryptic is swept. The two are not equivalent contexts, and the instrumented arm in defaults is what settles it — with I/L equated or not, the search examines about the same candidates (1.26M against 1.15M) and accepts about the same share of them (10.7% against 11.0%), and the binary-search/range-scan split barely moves (46/54 against 42/58). Under tryptic all three change at once: 9x fewer candidates, acceptance down to ~2%, and the split inverts to 86/14. So tryptic is a different workload and earns its multiplication; equate_il is the same workload with a different answer, which is a question for defaults and nowhere else. Crossing it here cost 45% of the whole sweep and moved a resolved k-mer winner in 2 of 23 contexts.

Suite notes

The one suite that varies the query count, because everywhere else it has to be fixed: two cells that ran different stream lengths are not comparable, so a suite holding everything else constant must hold this constant too. Here it IS the variable.

The mechanism is occupancy. search_all_matching_suffixes splits its input with par_chunks(tuning.mlp_batch), so a call of N peptides produces N / mlp_batch rayon tasks. At the 10,000 every other suite measures, that is 625 tasks and the machine is saturated. At a realistic 50-peptide request it is three, and on a twelve-core box nine cores idle for the whole call. Retrieval has the same shape: it parallelises over the peptides that matched.

So every throughput figure in this report is an upper bound taken at the one call size that guarantees full occupancy, and this suite is what says how far below it a real request lands. The number to take away is the KNEE — the smallest call size that reaches within the floor of the saturated figure. That is a number for client documentation, and it is not 10,000.

Per-rep wall time varies enormously down this sweep: the small cells run few queries and finish in milliseconds, so their bands are wide. Read the resolution table and the per-cell band before any delta near the bottom of the range.

equate_il is HELD at the shipped value here; only tryptic is swept. The two are not equivalent contexts, and the instrumented arm in defaults is what settles it — with I/L equated or not, the search examines about the same candidates (1.26M against 1.15M) and accepts about the same share of them (10.7% against 11.0%), and the binary-search/range-scan split barely moves (46/54 against 42/58). Under tryptic all three change at once: 9x fewer candidates, acceptance down to ~2%, and the split inverts to 86/14. So tryptic is a different workload and earns its multiplication; equate_il is the same workload with a different answer, which is a question for defaults and nowhere else. Crossing it here cost 45% of the whole sweep and moved a resolved k-mer winner in 2 of 23 contexts.

Suite notes

Load time is a property of one invocation, not of a rep, so every configuration is loaded once with a trivial query workload and the numbers come from the harness's own startup section. There is nothing to gain from running this at 100 reps.

Preloading a structure does not make its cost go away — it moves it from page faults spread across the steady state into one bulk copy at startup. Compare the total column, never the load column alone, and read this suite together with the throughput the same configuration reaches in ram.

PAGE CACHE, read before interpreting: after the first configuration has run, the index files are in the page cache, so every later load is doing memcpy rather than disk I/O. That is the right number for "how long does a restart take on a warm box" and the WRONG one for "how long does the first boot after a deploy take". Pass --cold (needs root) for the latter, and expect the sweep to take much longer.

The preloaded arm has nothing mapped to touch, so its page-touch warmup degrades to a small pipeline warmup automatically; its warmup column is therefore not comparable with the mapped arms'.

Suite notes

The storage-axes A/B put preloaded-proteins 21.5% ahead — but it ran with the whole index resident, which is the one regime where mmap has no advantage to show. Preloaded metadata is non-evictable anonymous memory, so under pressure it displaces file-backed cache for the suffix array and the mapping, both bigger and hotter per query. This sweeps the ceiling down and looks for the crossover.

Read the columns in this order:

  • slots is the gap between a cell's own two invocations. A delta smaller than it is not an answer for that ceiling — that is the lesson from the storage-axes run, where the real effects had 0.1-2.1% spreads and the noise had 6.8-12.9%.
  • drift is the first quarter of reps against the last. A capped cell begins with the cache the page sweep left behind and climbs; a large positive drift means it had not reached steady state, so its median understates that arm. Both arms drifting similarly is fine.
  • majflt is the mechanism. If throughput falls while major faults stay flat, residency is not what changed and something else is being measured (reclaim CPU, huge-page breakup).
  • RSS GB should track the ceiling once constrained. If it does not, the cap did not apply and the cell is void — check that the page cache was actually dropped.

--no-theoretical-memory is on for every cell. That calculation walks every protein's metadata, which on an mmap backend faults the whole metadata section in before anything is timed: it would pre-warm exactly what the mmap arm should be faulting on demand, and spend the budget being measured.

The 6-mer table is attached to both arms. It removes the top ~21 of ~34 binary-search probes, which is exactly the phase that degrades under a cap, so a sweep with it and a sweep without it answer different questions. Under a ceiling the 6-mer is +18.4% and -27.9% major faults against no table where a 5-mer is +3.2% / -6.2% — the table's value here is working-set size (~1 SA page per query at k=6 against ~7 at k=5), not probe count, and that only matters once pages can be evicted.

MADV_WILLNEED over the SA range was swept here and has since been removed from the searcher: the advice lands (majflt -23-25%) but buys nothing above the core count, and costs 3.7% resident. See the comment where it lived in sa-index/src/array/mmap.rs before re-opening that question. The reading rule generalises to anything readahead-shaped — check majflt before qps: majflt down with minflt up means the advice landed; majflt flat means it never took effect and any qps change is syscall cost or noise.

Suite notes

A major fault blocks its thread, and a CPU prefetch hint cannot fault, so once pages stop being resident the index's memory-level-parallelism machinery is inert and every miss idles a core. Oversubscription overlaps those stalls instead of removing them.

Established by the sweeps this suite replaces: oversubscription costs about 10% unconstrained and gains +65.3% at a 167G ceiling and +94.4% at 112G — a deployment knob, not a default, whose value scales with the fault rate. At 167G the curve is monotonic downward from 96 (96 > 128 > 192), so the peak is at or below 96. Major faults stayed flat across thread counts (0.24% spread).

Read it this way:

  • majflt should stay FLAT across thread counts at a given ceiling. Threads change how many faults are in flight, not how many there are. If it moves, something else changed too.
  • unconstrained is the go/no-go for making a thread count the default: with no faults to hide, oversubscription is pure context-switch overhead. If it costs there, it stays a deployment knob.
  • If the optimum at the tighter ceiling is higher than at the looser one, the rule is "scale threads with the fault rate", not a fixed number.
  • pprot vs mmap should hold the same sign across every thread count at a ceiling. Oversubscription hides faults; it does not remove them, so if the arms' fault COUNTS still differ while their throughput gap closes, the win is being overlapped rather than eliminated — and it will reopen on slower storage.

The grid is deliberately modest, since the peak is already bracketed at <= 96. Widen threads to bracket it more finely, or add ceilings, at the cost of roughly an hour per cell on the full database.
